newsitem.title: JAPAN: Pacific Century group grabs prime Tokyo land.
newsitem.headline: Pacific Century group grabs prime Tokyo land.

text.p: A tract of Tokyo prime land was auctioned off at nearly twice its expected price tag on Thursday, bought by the son of the one of the world's richest men.

Land located near Tokyo railway station was sold by JNR Settlement Corp to a Japanese unit of Pacific Century Group for 86.8 billion yen ($717 million), far higher than analysts' forecasts of a sum of 45 billion yen ($371 million).

Pacific Century Group is headed by Hong Kong-born businessman Richard Li who owns Pacific Century Regional Developments Ltd. He is the son of Li Ka-shing who owns the bluest of Hong Kong blue chips Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd.
"The price is out of this world. They must have really wanted this land," said Merrill Lynch real estate analyst Yukiaki Hayashi.
Hayashi said the price was 68 percent higher than what he had forecast.
Analysts said that while the sale could not be interpreted as anything but good for Japan's sluggish land market, participants were also likely to see it as an exceptional case.
They said Pacific Century Group had failed to win previous land auctions by JNR Settlement Corp and was eager to secure a piece of prime land.
But a spokesman for Pacific Century dismissed suggestions that it was desperate and had overpaid for the land.

"There are not many people that own land (in this area) and now we are one of them," he said. adding that the three previous land auctions by JNR Settlement Corp had all fetched higher than expected prices.
The group plans to develop an office building and lease it, he said.
While earlier auctions of prime land that had gone better than expected had cheered the Tokyo stock market, in particular its banking sector, analysts said it was unlikely to happen this time.
"Its out of the ordinary. I think the stock market is going to take this calmly," said Hisanori Ito, an analyst at Nikko Research Center.
Most Japanese banks are struggling with mountainous bad loans, many of which were made to the real estate sector and used property as collateral.
But analysts said the continued participation of foreign investors in the market would likely cheer up domestic participants.
"It will have a good pyschological effect and Japanese investors may think its alright to buy too," said Nikko Research's Ito.
Alderney Investment Pte Ltd, a Singpaorean firm, was part of a group that successfully bid last month for tracts of prime land near Ginza, Tokyo's premier shopping district.
